newsitem.title: USA: CSCE cocoa soars to new 7-month highs, specs buy.
newsitem.headline: CSCE cocoa soars to new 7-month highs, specs buy.

text.p: CSCE cocoa futures rallied to fresh seven-month highs on Monday, bolstered by chart-driven speculative buying, floor sources said.
"There is a lot of new spec buying and it is mainly technical," one trader said.
"You would have to have a lot of nerve to sell this market right now," he added.
Most-active May futures surged $42 a tonne on the day, to close at $1,482, after ranging from $1,490 to $1,422. July, which hit a new life-of-contract high, finished up $40, to $1,504.
The rest rose $36 to $40. Sept '97, Dec '97, Mar '98 and Dec '98 also set fresh contract highs.
Trade selling on the heels of London's early losses pushed prices some $18 a tonne lower early Monday, but local short-covering at the lows turned the market around, dealers said.
Upward momentum accelerated after the May contract breached $1,450, activating buy-stops, they said.
Technically, dealers said May was likely to face psychological resistance at the $1,500 level, while no major selling was expected until May broke below $1,420.
Today's gains came despite Friday's CFTC Commitment of Traders report, which showed speculators were net long over 17,000 lots as of March 11 after being net short just two weeks ago.

"Even though the specs now hold a sizeable long position, it looks like they still have more to buy," one trader said. "And as long as the market keeps going up and up, they're going to continue to buy."
Fundamentally, some traders said an expected world cocoa deficit of some 150,000 tonnes in 1996/97 underpinned prices.
"The fundamentals are coming into play here," a trader said. "There is a possible deficit and the Ivory Coast mid-crop may not be as good as people expected."
One leading UK-based analyst said on Monday the Ivorian mid-crop could be below average at around 100,000 tonnes due to exceptionally dry weather in February.
He put the total 1996/97 harvest at 1.070 million tonnes, including about 970,000 tonnes main crop.
Last week, Commodities Minister Guy-Alain Gauze said the total Ivorian crop would be less than one million tonnes.
An estimated 11,368 lots changed hands on the day, compared with Friday's official total of 11,331 lots.
